Thank you, Madam President. Madam President, Madam Executive Secretary, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, on behalf of the regional implementation annex for Central and Eastern Europe, I would like to express our sincere gratitude to the government and people of Mongolia for their warm hospitality and for the successful organization of the 17th session of the Conference of the Parties. We also extend our appreciation to the Secretariat for its professionalism and smooth coordination throughout the conference. The theme of this conference, Restoring Land, Restoring Hope, has served as a guiding principle for our common work. We are pleased that the discussions here in Ulaanbaatar reaffirmed yet again that land restoration is not merely an environmental objective, but an investment in food security, water availability, resilient livelihoods, and sustainable development. Annex V welcomes collective efforts to address land degradation and drought as we're leaving Ulaanbaatar with renewed commitment to multilateralism. We are particularly pleased that COP17 has reaffirmed the importance of engaging all parties in preventing land degradation and strengthening drought resilience, regardless of their climatic classification. We also welcome the attention given to rangelands and pastoralist communities, particularly in the context of the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists. Science-based approaches, innovation, and international cooperation remain essential to addressing these interconnected challenges. Our region highly appreciates the Commission's continued efforts to strengthen capacity building for parties. Our experience has shown that sustained demand-driven support is essential to strengthen both institutional and technical capacities. This includes access to data and technologies, project development and investment planning, as well as monitoring and reporting. We encourage the UNCCD to continue investing in practical training, technical assistance and knowledge exchange so that countries are better equipped to translate international commitments into concrete and measurable action at the national level. We highly appreciate the UNCCD's continued efforts to promote meaningful youth engagement, including through initiatives such as the Land Use Negotiation Program and Land Hero. These initiatives provide valuable opportunities for young people to learn, engage and contribute to the Convention. We encourage the UNCCD to further strengthen these opportunities and ensure that youth participation remains a meaningful and permanent part of the Convention's work. Annex V supports efforts to strengthen women's negotiation skills and technical capacities, enabling their effective participation in national delegations and contributing to more inclusive and effective decision making under the UNCCD Women's Delegates Fund. We also appreciate the continued support for strengthening civil society organizations, local communities, and other relevant stakeholders in land restoration and drought resilience. We welcome the strong attention given to drought resilience. The experience of Annex V countries demonstrates that drought is no longer an exceptional event, but an increasingly recurrent and complex risk. We therefore encourage the Convention and its partners to further support Parties in moving from reactive drought response towards proactive drought risk management and resilience, including through practical tools, knowledge exchange, capacity building and improved access to finance. In this regard, we recognize the value of the UNCCD communities of learning and practice on drought management as a platform for sharing experiences, strengthening capacities, and promoting practical solutions, as well as cooperation among countries and stakeholders. Distinguished delegates, land degradation neutrality remains a key framework for our collective efforts. We call for accelerated implementation of national LDN targets with strengthened action on restoration, sustainable land management, and the conservation of terrestrial ecosystems. These efforts should reflect diverse ecosystems and national circumstances while delivering tangible benefits for people, livelihood, and resilient landscapes. As we close the scope, we believe that our collective work must continue with the hope that our commitments will be translated into concrete action at all levels. This requires stronger science and data, improved monitoring of land and soil, enhanced drought preparedness and early warning systems, and continued support to Parties in reaching their targets. The main task ahead is therefore implementation. We therefore call for continued efforts to improve access to existing financial mechanisms, and mobilize additional resources for land restoration, drought resilience and sustainable land management. Available financing should be accessible, predictable and better aligned with national priorities and implementation needs. Annex V remains fully committed to this work and stands ready for active and constructive cooperation throughout the post COP17 process. I thank you, Madam President.

Madam President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, colleagues. As we bring this COP17 to a close, the European Union and its member states would like first to acknowledge the huge efforts made throughout this conference by the Mongolian Presidency to deliver meaningful progress on this critical issue. The challenges addressed by this convention are becoming more urgent and affect virtually every country and community. Protecting and restoring our land strengthening resilience to drought and improving the lives and livelihoods of people around the world are shared responsibilities. They require a strong UNCCD and effective multilateral cooperation. We came to Ulaanbaatar ready to engage, negotiate and compromise with the ambition of reaching balanced, concrete and implementable outcomes. We are encouraged that the same positive and constructive approach is shared by so many parties to this vitally important convention. We have been impressed and encouraged by the strong international collective will to drive forward an ambitious agenda to address the challenges of land degradation, desertification and drought. We are therefore concerned that on a number of issues, This COP has not been able to deliver the level of ambition and clarity that the circumstances require. Throughout these negotiations, the European Union and its member states have approached the process in a spirit of compromise and with a genuine desire to find solutions. We have listened to partners, engaged across negotiating groups and sought to bridge differences. We recognize that many other parties have done the same. At the same time, it's clear that the necessary convergence could not be achieved on a number of fundamental issues. The European Union and its member states are particularly concerned that on several issues of importance, it was not possible even to commence substantive discussion. This has made it extremely difficult to identify common ground and ultimately to reach consensus. Multilateralism depends on our willingness to engage with issues even when our positions differ. It cannot deliver when differences become a zero-sum exercise or when opportunities for substantive dialogue are not fully exploited. We therefore encourage all parties to remain open to meaningful dialogue, compromise and substantive discussion. This is not simply a matter of negotiating technique. It is essential to the credibility and effectiveness of the multilateral process. We regret in particular the missed opportunity to strengthen synergies among the three Rio Conventions. Land, climate and biodiversity challenges are deeply interconnected and in order to be truly effective, our responses must be interconnected too. Greater coherence and cooperation between the conventions are essential if we're to make the best use of limited resources and deliver meaningful results for countries and communities. The European Union will continue to support efforts by the UNFCCC and CBD to integrate these agendas, including through the existing platforms and processes for cooperation between the three Rio Conventions. On drought, while we had hoped for a more ambitious outcome, we welcome the decision to continue the conversation on future action on proactive drought management. Drought is intensifying in frequency, severity and impacts across regions of the world. Continuing the conversation is important, but it must lead also to action. And we therefore hope this work will enable us to develop a collective response commensurate with the urgency and scale of the challenge. We are pleased we found consensus over the budget. We would have preferred a budget providing more leeway and security for the future. but we think that the outcome allows the convention secretariat to continue its essential work for all parties. We look forward to all parties making timely contributions to the convention budget. We regret that the COP17 decisions have not given sufficient recognition to the importance of gender equality and the meaning participation and leadership of women and girls. We cannot achieve land degradation neutrality without gender equality. Women and girls are key agents of change in sustainable land management, land restoration and drought resilience. Gender responsive and transformative approaches must therefore remain integral to the implementation of the convention. The same is true of broader participation of stakeholders. The Convention is stronger when the voices and contributions of civil society, indigenous peoples, local communities, youth, women, farmers and other stakeholders are heard. Their participation is not an optional extra. It is essential to effective implementation on the ground, and we must continue to ensure that our processes reflect this reality. Madam President, it is important that we are candid about where we stand. The outcome of this COP is not due to a lack of ambition or engagement on the part of the European Union. Yet, we have not been able to reach all the outcomes we'd hoped for. And we should not allow disappointment to obscure what unites the vast majority of us. The work does not stop here. Between now and COP18, the European Union and its Member States will continue to engage constructively, seek common ground and work towards meaningful progress on drought, finance, the Convention's budget, gender equality, inclusive participation and stronger synergies across the Rio Conventions. We remain committed to advancing the unfinished business of this COP and to building the convergence necessary to achieve further results at COP18. Madam President, the European Union and its Member States express their sincere appreciation of the Mongolian Presidency for its leadership and unstinting efforts throughout this COP. We recognise the considerable work, commitment and patience that the Presidency has invested in trying to bring parties together, often under very challenging circumstances. We are equally grateful for the extraordinary hospitality extended to all of us by the Mongolian people. We have been warmly welcomed in Ulaanbaatar, And we will leave Mongolia with a great appreciation for its generosity, its culture, and the spirit with which it has hosted this important conference. In closing, we remain fully committed to the UN Convention to Combat Desertification and to effective multilateral cooperation. While we have not reached all that we set out to achieve in Ulaanbaatar, the urgency of the challenges before us have not diminished. If anything, it has increased our resolve. Let us therefore leave this COP with a clear grasp on why we have not been able to deliver on a higher level of ambition. Let us also leave with renewed determination to preserve the spirit of multilateralism, to engage meaningfully where differences remain, and to turn the unfinished businesses of COP17 into meaningful progress. The European Union and its member states will remain a constructive partner in that effort. Thank you, Mrs. President.

Thank you, Madam President. Madam Executive Secretary, distinguished delegates, as COP17 is approaching to a close, Egypt wishes to convey its deep appreciation to the government and people of Mongolia, to the COP17 presidency team, and to the UNCCD Secretariat for their collective leadership, dedication, and hospitality throughout this session. Egypt would like to take this opportunity to reiterate its sincere appreciation to all parties for the trust and confidence placed in Egypt as host of the 18th session of the Conference of the Parties to the UN Convention to Combat Desertification. The significance of COP17 lies not only in the decisions adopted during these two weeks, but also in the collective political message that has emerged from Ulaanbaatar. Under the theme of restoring land, restoring hope, parties have reaffirmed that healthy land is fundamental to sustainable development, economic prosperity, social stability and resilience. Above all, this conference has reminded us that the work of restoring land is also the work of restoring hope. Hope for communities facing the realities of drought and degradation, hope for more resilient livelihoods, and hope for a more secure and sustainable future. Parties have also reaffirmed that addressing desertification, land degradation, and drought requires collective action and international solidarity. In an increasingly complex world, this message carries particular importance. Multilateralism is not an abstract principle. It is the practical recognition that the challenges we face transcend borders and require solutions that no nation can achieve alone. The UNCCD should continue to demonstrate the value of dialogue, cooperation and consensus building in advancing common objectives and supporting those countries most vulnerable to environmental and development pressures. For many developing countries, drought and land degradation are not future risks. They are present day realities affecting communities, economies and development prospects. Our collective responsibility is therefore clear to accelerate implementation, strengthen resilience, support affected communities and ensure that communities are matched and ensure that commitments are matched by the necessary means of implementation. As incoming presidency of COP18, Egypt is committed to working closely with current presidency, all parties, regional groups, non-party stakeholders, and all partners in the spirit that has characterized this conference. We will build on the momentum generated in Riyadh COP16 and strengthened here in Ulaanbaatar to advance an inclusive, transparent, and action-oriented process. We see COP18 as an opportunity not only to advance the implementation of the convention, but also to further elevate the desertification, land degradation and drought agenda within the global sustainable development framework. Our ambition is to contribute to a COP that delivers practical outcomes, strengthens partnerships, and reinforces the central role of land restoration and drought resilience in achieving sustainable development. As Mongolia passes the torch to Egypt, we do so united by a shared conviction that restoring land is an investment in people, investment in resilience, and investment in the future we seek to build together. Let us carry forward the spirit of cooperation and continue our journey towards COP18 with renewed determination, ambition and confidence in the power of multilateral action. I thank you.

Madam President, Executive Secretary, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, on behalf of Annex II, the Asia Pacific Group, India has the honor to address the closing session of the 17th session of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification. Let me begin by extending our deepest condolences to the government of Nepal, China and India and all the families affected by the devastating flash floods. Our thoughts are with the communities grieving the tragic loss of lives and we stand in steadfast solidarity with the nations as rescue and recovery efforts continue. Madam President, We commend you and your team for your leadership and the tireless efforts to facilitate consensus. We thank the government and the people of Mongolia for the generous hospitality. We also thank the Executive Secretary, the UNCCD Secretariat, the Global Mechanism, the Chairs and Bureau of the Subsidiary Bodies, the facilitators of the contact groups, interpreters, conference services, security personnel, and all partners who supported our work. We acknowledge the continued contribution of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia as the COP16 presidency and thank all parties for the constructive spirit demonstrated throughout these negotiations. Madam President, distinguished delegates, the Asia-Pacific Group recognizes the considerable work undertaken throughout COP17. For our region, key priorities have included the future strategic direction of the Convention. drought resilience, sand and dust storms, effective reporting and implementation through CRIC, capacity building, a robust and realistic budget, resource mobilization, and strong scientific and technical support through the CST and the SPI. Across these areas, adequate means of implementation, capacity building, and strengthened regional and international cooperation remain essential. We welcome that the Secretariat will continue to support the convening of all UNCCD caucuses. The Asia Pacific Group reiterates the global and transboundary nature of drought and sand and dust storms, different nature and drivers of land degradation due to diverse geographical context and the need to have cooperation with the national, regional, inter-regional and international organizations to address these challenges, enhance financial resources and transfer of technology. Our region also reflects unique and diverse circumstances, home to most of the world's population and spanning high mountains and forests, agriculture plains, dry lands and deserts, low-lying atolls, range lands, deltas, coasts, and small island developing states. Across these landscapes, our ecosystems are deeply interconnected from land and forest to freshwater and oceans. For many countries, particularly SIDS, what happens on land directly affects surrounding ecosystem, communities, and livelihoods. Recognizing these connections will be essential to effective implementation of the convention. Madam President, COP17 has demonstrated that cross-cutting and procedural matters can have significant implications for progress across the convention. Issues including gender, synergies among the Rio conventions, seats, indigenous people and local communities, as well as stakeholder participation have arisen across multiple agenda items. Going forward, we should consider more effective ways to address these recurring matters. Similarly, procedural clarity, inclusive participation and equitable reasonable representation are fundamental to effective negotiations. The experience of this COP highlights the need to strengthen our approaches so that procedural challenges can be addressed early and constructively, allowing parties to focus their time and energy on substantial outcomes and implementation. Our region welcomes the commitment and initiatives launched during COP17, including the Steppe Action Agenda, the Interregional Initiative to Combat Sand and Dust Storms in Western Asia, as well as the willingness of many Parties to establish an International Day of Rangeland and Pastoralism. Yet, we deeply regret that this unprecedented situation has prevented meaningful consideration of critical matters at COP17. Restoring hope requires respect, not imposition. Consensus must be built through negotiation, engagement and compromise. We urge parties to ensure that this regression does not become a precedent. Gender, civil society participation, including the participation of the indigenous and local communities caucuses, as well as synergies among the Rio Conventions must all be on the COP18 agenda. We are also disappointed at the low attendance of parties at the open dialogue sessions and the gender caucus session, as well as repeated program modifications that limited the effectiveness of these spaces. Meaningful dialogue requires parties to be present. Our substantive messages must also be heard. On drought, we call for proactive, inclusive, and human rights-based approaches supporting healthy landscapes, sustainable food systems, and locally led resilience. On rangelands, pastoralism and mobility must be recognized as resilient and adaptive systems with the secure tenure rights, meaningful participation and direct support for pastoralist communities. Statement from the International Forum of Indigenous Peoples. on the UNCCD COP17 28 August 2026 thank you Madam President my name is Sonia Astua Manpardeva and I address you on behalf of the Indigenous Peoples Caucus we the International Forum for the Indigenous Peoples of the United Nations Convention against Desertification reaffirm our commitment to protect our lands and territories, cultures and knowledge systems for present and future generations. Our lands have been subjected to growing pressure owing to desertification, degradation, drought, climate change, biodiversity loss and unsustainable development. And yet we, the indigenous peoples, continue to protect, restore and sustain our lands and territories through our knowledge, customary governance and generations of stewardship. We are not merely affected by these crises. We are rights holders, knowledge holders, custodians and solution providers. We recall decision 5/COP16, which established the basis for the creation of an indigenous peoples caucus and strengthened the recognition of indigenous peoples differentiated participation in UN CCD processes. We call upon the parties to start operationalization of the terms of reference of the Indigenous Peoples Caucus as decided upon at COP16. We further reaffirm the principles and rights enshrined in the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, as well as other international instruments, including rights to self-determination, full and effective participation in decision-making processes on lands, territories, resources, knowledge systems and our livelihoods. Having recognised the efforts of those states that have established secure land tenure and have acknowledged the collective land rights of indigenous peoples, we urge all states to adopt similar measures, particularly by recognizing and safeguarding land tenure and the collective rights of indigenous peoples to our lands, territories and resources, consistent with decision 26/COP14. We call for the equitable and ethical integration of indigenous peoples' knowledge systems alongside scientific knowledge, in the CST and UNCCD policies, programs and decision making at the same time guaranteeing protection of our knowledge, intellectual property rights and indigenous data sovereignty. We plead for guaranteeing direct, flexible, accessible, equitable and non-discriminatory finance for indigenous peoples and indigenous-led organizations without unnecessary intermediaries. Our rights, our knowledge, our territories, our leadership, restore land, restore rights, restore hope. Thank you.

Fellow young people, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, we are not here today to speak about the distant future. We are here to speak about the future we are already living because the one we are inheriting is at risk. Like many, we are deeply frustrated that since the adoption of the agenda, key issues were blocked from consideration by a few parties. preventing these issues from being addressed at this COP, which undermined existing commitments and continues to delay the urgent action our communities can no longer afford to wait for. We recognize and appreciate the many parties who stood with civil society, indigenous peoples, women, youth, pastoralists and local communities and equally supported the consideration of these issues. Your voices will continue to count beyond COP17. But our message today goes beyond the agenda. We call on Parties to institutionalize youth participation by ensuring young people are meaningfully involved in national processes, including national action programs and land degradation neutrality strategies, from design through implementation, monitoring and evaluation. Fully implement the youth engagement strategy. We need the youth engagement strategy to move from a global commitment to concrete action at national and regional levels. Direct accessible resources for frontline youth. Young people need dedicated non-debt financing, technical support, mentorship and capacity building with funding that is accessible to youth-led and locally-led organizations. Recognize land as a living system. Land can't be separated from food, water, biodiversity, health, livelihoods, culture, and peace. Restoration must be holistic, regenerative, and grounded in soil health. Protect pastoralism and local knowledge. Restoration must recognize the expertise of indigenous peoples, local communities, and pastoralists, and measure success through genuine ecosystem recovery, not simply the number of trees planted. Build genuine government youth partnership. Young people must be recognized not only as participant, but as partners and implementers. Invest in intergenerational learning and capacity building, equipping young people with knowledge, skills and networks to translate global commitments into actions. And strengthen youth participation must be measured not only by how many young people sit in a room, but how many have a voice in decisions and how many see that voice reflected in action. And finally, we call for stronger youth coordination within the UNCCD Secretariat, including consideration of a dedicated youth staff position to strengthen communication, access and implementation of the youth engagement strategy. Excellencies, we need to be honest about what is at stake. Every year of inaction is not a neutral year. Every delayed decision has a cost. Every compromise that postpones action on land degradation, desertification, and drought pushes that cost onto our generation. If we continue to debate while our soils are degraded, our systems are under pressure, our lands become less productive, and droughts become more devastating, what exactly are we asking young people to inherit? A world where fertile land is increasingly scarce, A world where food and water insecurity fuel displacement and conflict. A world where livelihoods disappear before young people even have the opportunity to build them. A world where our generation is forced to spend its future managing crises created by decades of indecision. That can't be the legacy of this convention. Young people are not asking to inherit a better future. We are asking for the political courage, resources, and and space to help build it. The decisions made in this room will help shape lands we inherit, the food we eat, the livelihoods we build, and the communities we call home. So let COP17 not be remembered for the issues that were prevented from being discussed. Let it be remembered for the moment when this convention recognized that inaction in itself is a decision and that our generation will live with the consequences of every decision made here. Let COP17 be remembered for the courage to listen, the commitment to act, and the decision to put young people at the heart of restoring our land. Our generation is ready. Our communities are ready. Our lands cannot wait. The question is no longer whether we can act. The question is whether you will choose to act before the cost of inaction becomes a future none of us can afford. I thank you all.

I regret that we were not able to reach an agreement on gender. As a woman, I feel this particularly deeply. Because the full and meaningful participation of women is not only a matter of principle, it's essential to the resilience of the people, livelihood of the community, and the land we are here to store. The people closest to the land cannot be treated simply as beneficiary of decisions made elsewhere. These are the right holder, they are the knowledge holder, and partners in implementation. Our measure of success today is not simply what we are adopting, but the change of these decisions and how they can be reflected on land. We have an ambition, and this had to be met with the means of implementation and translated on the ground. But also implementation requires functioning of a secretariat. The ambition entrusted in this convention with those decisions and decisions more to come, would require that this budget that has been adopted, that the parties would fulfill their contribution in due time so that we would be able to deliver what we promised you to deliver. Thanks to the negotiators and to the chairs and facilitators of the governing body, you've done a wonderful job with us. And congratulations to the new chairs of our governing bodies. And rest assured that the secretariat would stand ready to support your work in the coming two years. I express deepest appreciation to everyone here who has stayed very late and who has been always pushing forward in order that these negotiations would continue. I'd like to thank the Bureau and the COP17 presidency for your leadership and patience and determination and meeting every day in order to follow up on that. It is that kind of persistence that makes the multilateral system moving. To our indigenous people, local communities, and women and girls, and most important, our youth that we heard today, thank you for your speeches, for continuing to remind us who and what these negotiations are all about. It's about people, livelihood and dignity, and the future that you own. And for that reason, the Secretariat has agreed with the COP16 Presidency on a funding of what's called the Riyadh Action Agenda in order to continue the work and provide financial resources. I do invite parties who are interested to that to continue with us our journey from COP17 to COP18. And finally, to the UNCCD team that is here in this room and those who were not able to join us but worked as our backbone in the Bonn office. I'd like to say a particular and heartfelt thank you. You have worked tirelessly, often under extraordinary pressure and stress, with very limited resources, whether in our number or how we are doing our function. Much of that work parties did not see it, but I did feel it and appreciate it greatly. Thank you for your professionalism, resilience, and for pushing through till the last minute in those difficult days. Thanks to the volunteers, because without you, it would have been difficult to be here. In Mongolia, they say, a good horse is not frightened by a long road, and we still have a long road that's difficult and long to go ahead with that. I'd like here. Also to reiterate that Mongolia has given us a lasting legacy of rangeland and pastoralism that we will carry over to COP18. And I would like to congratulate both Serbia and Egypt for hosting the upcoming CRIC and upcoming COP, and we look forward to work closely with both of them. And from here, implementation is not only about hectares and dollars. It's about the people that we will continue to serve. We're leaving Ulaanbaatar because it gave us the elements and architecture of implementation. And now we will move together to deliver this to COP18 and beyond. I thank you very much.

I thank the Executive Secretary of the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification. Excellencies, distinguished participants, we have now reached the end of the session. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, over the past two weeks, we have gathered in the National Park of Ulaanbaatar cradled in the valley of Tolt River and Balkhan Mountains, and oldest protected area in Mongolia. Those who protected this natural treasure were looking beyond themselves. And that call of our ancestors found a tangible reflection when over three decades ago, the world community came together to combat desertification under the UN Convention. Since then, our governments have gathered 17 times to renew their collective resolve and determination to protect our land, take effective national actions, support international cooperation towards sustainable development. This conference demonstrated once again the strong commitment of the parties, the mandate of the convention. distinguished delegation delegates COP 17 has delivered an important political outcome through the adoption of the Ulan Batar declaration reaffirming parties commitment to land degradation neutrality stronger implement implementation improved policy coherence International cooperation and greater access to Finance the conference also concluded decisions on range lands private sector engagement, sand and dust storms, the science policy interface, the future strategic framework of the convention through the IWG and drought. Taken together, these outcomes strengthen the policy and institutional foundation for implementation while placing people, livelihoods and country-led action more clearly at the center of land restoration, rangeland management, soil and water conservation and resilience. At the same time, COP17 demonstrated that implementation must be backed by real projects, partnerships and investment. The conference helped assemble a portfolio of 45 land restoration, rangeland and drought resilience project across 23 countries valued at about $1.3 billion, including the Rangelands Flagship Initiative and the Business for Land Hub of Mongolia. These developments have helped elevate rangelands and pastoralists within the global land agenda and strengthen the connection between policy ambition, finance, private sector engagement, and delivery on the ground. The task now is to carry this momentum forward and ensure that the decisions, partnerships, and investments advanced in Ulaanbaatar translate into healthier land, stronger livelihoods and measurable benefits for people and communities. Distinguished delegates, negotiations were not easy, but this is what makes our success even more satisfying. As a result of hard work, long days and deprived sleeps, we have ensured collective outcomes that represent our common priorities. Despite the differences of views on several items, parties were able to make an important progress on negotiations through sustained dialogue, flexibility, and shared commitment to the convention. These outcomes are close to our hearts, building on the momentum generated by the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists. We will remain committed to the advancement of the sustainable rangeland management, conservation and restoration, and inclusive rangeland governance. I'm encouraged by the adoption of the decision on the final report of the intergovernmental working group on the future strategic framework of the convention, the decision on drought and other important decisions. This demonstrates that consensus remains possible even on the most difficult issues, thanks to the parties' engagement, good faith and spirit of compromise. As we leave Ulaanbaatar, I hope that the spirit of solidarity and multilateral cooperation demonstrated during COP17.

Will continue to guide.

The implementation of the Convention and our collective efforts beyond this conference. As Presidency of the 17th Conference of the Parties to the UNCCD, we look forward to working with all of you over the next two years to continue strengthening this Convention, enhancing multilateral action and obtaining results on the ground. On behalf of the government of Mongolia and the COP17 presidency, I would like to express our deep gratitude to all parties and regional groups that demonstrated flexibility, patience and political will in helping us bridge differences and reach consensus. On behalf of the COP17 presidency, we convey our profound appreciation to the secretariat of the UNCCD, dear Yasmin, Andrea, Rajib, and all those who contributed to making these conferences a success. Also, I would like to thank our chairs of the committees and facilitators, Mr. Halid Cherki, Nicholas Webb, Philippine Dutai, Miss Charles Lang, Mr. Noel Joseph, Mr. Pujanraj Gurung, Miss Marina Medini, and I extend my sincere gratitude to the president Speaker and Prime Minister of Mongolia for their invaluable support and contribution to successful organization of COP17. My appreciation also goes to the National Preparatory Committee led by the Minister of Environment and Climate Change, COP17 Preparatory Office and all civil servants of ministries and government agencies for their close cooperation dedication and commitment throughout the preparation and conduct of this conference. I would equally like to recognize the contribution of international organizations, civil society organizations, the private sector, academia, youth, volunteers, interpreters, technicians, service personnel, and everyone who worked tirelessly behind the scenes. It has been a great honor and privilege for me to welcome you all to Ulaanbaatar. I wish you safe journey home.

I thank you. I hereby declare closed the 17th.
